questions.q: What is the programme mainly about?
options: Men who take their wife's family name when they marry
Countries where people cannot change their names
How couples choose names for their children
Why fewer people in the UK are getting married
questions.why: Dan says the topic is 'a husband taking a wife's name after marriage'.

questions.q: What happened with Dan's wife's surname?
options: She happily took Dan's name because she disliked her own
She kept her own name and Dan took it too
She wanted to keep it, but the law made her take Dan's
She made a double-barrelled name with both names
questions.why: Dan says his wife wanted to keep her surname but was forced to take his because of the law.

questions.q: According to Neil, where does the UK tradition of women taking the husband's name come from?
options: A law passed in France in 1789 after the revolution
The Norman idea that a wife became her husband's property
A religious rule brought over from the Middle East
A custom that began with the royal family in London
questions.why: Neil says it dates back to the Normans in 1066, who saw a married woman as the man's property.

questions.q: Why did Rory Dearlove take his wife's surname?
options: His wife asked him to do it
He wanted to protest against sexism
His old surname was hard to spell
He didn't feel strongly about his own name
questions.why: Neil says Rory wasn't really attached to his name, so it made no difference to him.

questions.q: What did the Opinium study of 2,000 UK adults suggest?
options: About one in ten young men fall into this group
Half of young men would refuse to change their name
Most women now keep their maiden names
Double-barrelled names are becoming less popular
questions.why: The study suggested that one in ten millennial men aged 18 to 34 fall into this category.

questions.q: Why did Charlie Shaw take his wife's name?
options: Because his teacher at school told him it was polite
Because his own family name was unusual and hard to spell
Because it was the law in the country where he married
To recognise the hidden bias against women in society
questions.why: He said it was a chance to acknowledge the unseen patriarchal bias and sexism in society.

questions.q: What did Rachel Robnett's research find?
options: Most people think couples should share one name
Husbands of women who keep their names are seen as 'feminine'
Women who change their names are seen as weaker
Men in the US are happier to change names than men in the UK
questions.why: She found these husbands are viewed as 'feminine', while the women are thought to 'wear the trousers'.

questions.q: What did most of the people Dan spoke to in London think?
options: A man should never take his wife's name
Only couples with children should share a name
People should be free to choose what they want
The tradition should be made into a law
questions.why: Neil says most of them said people are free to do what they want.
